source.title: HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
source.authors: Shei Pern Chua; Hao Wu; Qianli Ma; Fang-Zhao Wu

record.file_problem: None noted; the provided text includes the paper and appendices through the reported fine-tuning-attack results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmfulness and refusal as distinct directions and analyzes how they relate across token positions, layers, attacks, and model families. Its results refine the single-direction account rather than directly reproducing single-direction ablation or addition.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on ablating and adding a refusal direction but does not report its own test of that intervention. It uses refusal-direction ablation to obtain harmful continuations for extracting response-side directions; this is not reported as a test of refusal removal. HARC is a separately trained coupling method, not an ablation or addition of one direction. The paper reports attack projection signatures in figures, with the corresponding numerical values figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study extracts its own difference-in-means harmfulness and refusal directions at prompt and response positions. It reports their cosine geometry across layers and five instruct families, and projects successful DAN, PAIR and CodeAttack prompts onto them. These results bear on V5 (harm encoded apart from refusal) and on V3 (whether attacks suppress the refusal direction). It does not run its own ablation or addition test of refusal (V1); refusal-direction ablation is used only as a tool to generate harmful continuations. HARC is the authors' own method, and its results fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that harmfulness and refusal are separable directions at both prompt and response positions. Successful jailbreaks suppress the refusal or harm direction (or both) at the prompt side, yet harm recognition persists during generation. The four-direction structure replicates across five families, with directions extracted per model. HARC coupling improves robustness without capability or over-refusal costs, though it is broken by about 160 fine-tuning examples.
record.recipe_differences: The paper extracts difference-in-means directions but does not test the original single-direction refusal ablation/addition recipe. Its main intervention is LoRA fine-tuning with coupling losses on harmfulness and refusal directions at prompt and response positions.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction geometry varies by layer and architecture; the paper says four-direction structure can collapse onto a shared axis at other layers. Prompt-side decoupling varies across model families; Qwen response-side directions are more tightly coupled than Llama's. CodeAttack signatures differ between architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: HARC fine-tuning couples harm and refusal directions and cuts mean ASR (Llama 0.430→0.092; Qwen 0.632→0.133) with capability unchanged. It is undone by about 160 harmful fine-tuning examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training harm and refusal directions to co-activate improves jailbreak robustness at little capability cost, but is easily reversed by fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-side and response-side refusal directions are only partly aligned: cos 0.49 on Llama L27, 0.10 on Qwen L12, 0.30 on Qwen L27.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction is position-dependent, differing between instruction tokens and generated tokens.

record.problems: The main Table 1 comparisons are single-seed; three-seed results are reported for HARC only. Attack projection values are presented in figures, with categorical descriptions in the text. The authors note that the study does not evaluate adaptive attacks designed with knowledge of HARC, tests only selected model families and scales, and does not sweep several training hyperparameters.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted to meet the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No own test of ablating or adding the refusal direction on refusal rates or capability. Ablation is used only to generate harmful continuations.
No causal test that attacks work via the direction; projections are correlational and figure-only. No training against direction ablation. GCG is not analysed.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple refusal directions. The prompt- versus response-side refusal directions are a different construct.
No transfer of a fixed direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct. Directions are re-extracted per model.

missing.what: Response-side refusal-direction projections for attacks: DAN/PAIR recover refusal signal while complying; CodeAttack is negative on Llama L24–32 and near zero on Qwen.
Cross-layer prompt-side profiles: PAIR drives harm negative across nearly all layers; CodeAttack stays near zero throughout.
Per-family numerical cosine matrices for Mistral, Phi and Gemma; values are present but garbled in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The paper contradicts itself: its contributions say successful attacks 'suppress the refusal direction', but its own figure text says PAIR activates refusal. Attack projections are figure-only, in deltas, and for successful jailbreaks only, with no causal test. Section 3.1 is an analysis by the study; Arditi et al. is not re-tested.

versions.untested_parts: No own ablation of the single difference-in-means refusal direction to measure refusal removal, no addition to harmless prompts, and no matched test of general capability under those interventions.
No training against the direction's ablation; HARC trains to couple harmfulness and refusal directions instead. Attack analysis covers DAN, PAIR, and CodeAttack, not every jailbreak class.
The study analyzes distinct harmfulness and refusal directions and their position- and layer-dependent geometry, but does not compare affine, cone, and dominant-direction models directly.
The study measures separate harmfulness and refusal directions and projections, but does not independently assess the accuracy of a model's harmfulness judgment.
Cross-family transfer is tested for instruction-tuned models; transfer across languages, base-to-instruct stages, and other variants is not tested.
No comparison of when or how refusal training creates a removable direction.
